summary: Describes a way to write down and store IP routing policies in a routing registry, such as the RIPE database. It updates the earlier ripe-81 proposal, adds extensions suggested by Merit, and aims to be a common representation for all Internet routing registries. It serves as both tutorial and detailed reference.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks have rules about whose traffic they will carry. This memo is a shared notebook format so everyone can write those rules down the same way and others can read them.

questions: how are routing policies stored in a routing registry
how do networks announce routes to neighbors
subtitle: A standard format for networks to write and share their routing policies.

tldr.problem: Networks exchange traffic through complex rules, but had no common way to record or communicate those rules. Operators needed to coordinate policies but lacked a standard language.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1786 defines a database of objects (routes, autonomous systems, communities) where networks can publish what traffic they accept from or send to neighbors. The RIPE routing registry implements this, letting any operator query the policies of others.
tldr.outcome: The specification became the basis for Internet routing registries worldwide, enabling operators to document, share and even automatically check policies. It separates routing policy information from address allocation information in the database.

today: RFC 1786 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The RIPE-81++ routing policy representation became the foundation for Internet routing registries used today by RIPE, APNIC, AFRINIC, LACNIC, and ARIN. Modern routing registries still use object types derived from this specification to let operators record and query routing policies.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 1786 updates an earlier RIPE document known as ripe-81, building a standard way for Internet networks to describe and store their routing policies. Routing policies determine which networks a system accepts traffic from or announces routes to, but for decades these policies existed only in router configurations, invisible to other operators.

The RFC provides both a tutorial and detailed technical reference for a database of routing policy objects. It was built by combining ideas from RIPE (the European registry), Merit (a US network operator), and CERN. The document acts as the foundation for Internet routing registries worldwide, giving the global routing system a shared language for policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks have different rules about who they'll swap traffic with. This RFC is a rulebook everyone agreed to use, so when one network wants to know another's rules, they can look them up in a shared database.

sections.title: Routing Policies and Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
An Autonomous System (AS) is a group of networks operated by one organization with a single, clearly defined routing policy. Each AS has a unique number. Two ASes exchange routing information using exterior routing protocols like BGP.

A routing policy governs which networks an AS will accept announcements from or send announcements to. When AS X wants traffic from network NET1 to reach AS Y, AS X must first announce NET1 to AS Y, and then AS Y must accept that announcement. This is where policy comes in: an AS can refuse announcements from certain neighbors, or accept them with restrictions.

The RFC notes that with current destination-based forwarding, some reasonable policies cannot be implemented. For example, an AS cannot split traffic to the same destination based on the source address, because all traffic to one destination must follow the same path once the packets enter the AS.
sections.plainLanguage: An AS is a network with one main set of rules. Two ASes swap routing announcements: one says 'I can reach network X' and the other decides whether to believe it. Their policies control which announcements they exchange.

sections.title: The Routing Registry Objects
sections.content:
The RIPE database holds several object types for routing policy. The main ones are:

Route objects describe a single network announced into the Internet. A route object records the network prefix (like 192.87.45.0/24), the AS that originates it, and any communities it belongs to. The RFC separates routing information from address allocation: address blocks go into inetnum objects, while the routing policies go into separate route objects.

Autonomous System (aut-num) objects describe an AS and its routing policy. Each aut-num lists the neighboring ASes and what is announced to or accepted from each. This describes exactly the part of global policy that the AS controls locally.

AS-macro objects group multiple ASes so they can be referenced in policies as a unit. This is useful for policies that apply to a transit provider and all its customers.

Community objects group routes by criteria other than AS (for statistics, local policies, or non-routing uses). Unlike ASes, communities are not used for exterior routing decisions but can organize routes for management or auditing.
sections.plainLanguage: The database has entries for networks (routes), for network operators (ASes), for groups of operators (macros), and for other groupings (communities). Each entry says who maintains it and what its rules are.

sections.title: Route Objects and Aggregation
sections.content:
A route object represents a single announcement. The RFC explains how networks aggregate multiple smaller routes into larger ones to save router table space. This raises questions about policy when aggregates contain routes with different policies (heterogeneous aggregates).

For example, if one network (193.0.8.0/24) belongs to community SPECIAL and another (193.0.9.0/24) does not, aggregating both into 193.0.8.0/23 makes it impossible for other ASes to accept only the special routes without also accepting the regular ones. The RFC introduces attributes for this: withdrawn marks routes that are no longer announced but whose policies must be remembered, and hole lists prefixes within an aggregate that are not reachable through the announcer. Documenting holes helps operators debug connectivity problems faster.

The RFC emphasizes that route objects are strictly controlled: only the AS that originates a route can add or modify its route object. This gives operators control over their own routing announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network announces a large route that includes multiple smaller routes with different rules, the database can note which parts have which rules, or mark parts as no longer active. This helps other networks understand what traffic really flows where.

sections.title: Expressing Routing Policy
sections.content:
The RFC describes how network operators use these objects to express policy in practice. Each aut-num object lists neighboring ASes and specifies for each neighbor what the AS announces (sends) and what it accepts (receives). Since each AS controls only its own side of the exchange, the global routing graph comes from combining all aut-num objects.

The RFC includes extensive examples showing how to represent different scenarios: a single network and its routes, aggregated routes, networks multihomed to multiple ASes, and proxy aggregation where one AS announces routes on behalf of customers. The detailed syntax for each object type is provided in appendices.

The document also covers access policies (blocking specific source-destination pairs) and explains the transition from the earlier ripe-81 representation, acknowledging that operators would need to migrate existing policy descriptions to the new format.
sections.plainLanguage: In the database, each network lists its neighbors and says what routes it sends to each and accepts from each. By reading all these lists, anyone can figure out the whole network of routing decisions.
